extracted.intended_audience: university administrators, instructional designers, faculty, and technical staff responsible for planning and operating online learning
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning, governing, resourcing, and operating online learning systems in post-secondary institutions, including human resources, change management, governance, communication, pilot evaluation, and choice/use of learning technologies. Focus is on institutional-level infrastructure and practical technologies for course delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear lines of responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: lines of responsibility must be in place to avoid duplication of effort or gaps in support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define roles so tasks are neither duplicated nor neglected; explicit responsibilities reduce gaps in student support and technical/administrative coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human resource policies and employment conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: A host of human resource issues need to be addressed. Some are tied to collective agreement and employment contract terms and conditions, especially those related to service standards and expectations (which go beyond the normal working day) and the automatic flexibility that online learning provides not only to the student, but also to the staff in terms of the place and times that they work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop policies that account for online-specific duties (chatting, forum moderation, blogging, podcasting, wiki editing), attendance expectations, standards for being in touch with central offices, and how online work fits existing agreements and contracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staff training, hiring, classification and career development
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional approaches to hiring, appointment, promotions, position classification, access to training and professional development have to be adapted in order to maximize the opportunity to invest in and reward staff in such a dynamic environment, and/or to avoid exploiting staff who may be working well above the level for which they are paid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide flexible, inter/intra-institutional training, support groups, and learning communities; adapt recruitment and promotion criteria to recognize online-learning skills and to retain staff who develop into key online roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision-making and resource-allocation processes
rubrics_metrics.description: The process for decision-making and resource allocation related to online learning in an institution or organization must be carefully considered. If new committees are to be established ... care must be taken to balance the discussion between those who know and understand a lot ..., central technical staff, decentralized technical staff ..., the central administration ..., and the users (teachers and learners).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish processes that balance expert advice with administrative accountability and user perspectives; incorporate independent and thorough evaluation into decision-making about investments and direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational capacity to manage change
rubrics_metrics.description: The organization’s capacity and capability of effectively managing change is of vital importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for the impacts of curricular, technological, and student expectation changes; recognize that changes in online systems can have wide-reaching effects and therefore require organizational capability to manage them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between innovation and stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance: specifically, between every time a new idea or product comes into view ... versus sticking with an established system (typically for administrative ease and staff convenience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh benefits of adopting new systems against administrative burden and staff convenience; avoid frequent switching to unproven solutions and consider lifecycle and support implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralization versus decentralization considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of centralization or decentralization of a system (or systems) also drives the change process. To what extent will some units be free to explore and try new systems, and to what extent will those lagging behind be forced to update their approaches?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions about central control affect innovation, standardization, support burdens, and equity; resolve these within the organization’s culture and business context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership that embraces change
rubrics_metrics.description: Having the right attitude towards change, its importance and value, is essential. Change should be embraced, and not seen to be just another headache to be dealt with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders (especially in consensual cultures like universities) must understand diverse stakeholder needs and be able to guide and champion change rather than impose it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scouting reports and engagement with development communities
rubrics_metrics.description: Some staff ... must look around for emerging trends and ideas in online learning systems, and provide a place for others to feed information they come across. These scouting reports need to be compiled and shared. Staff ... need to incorporate themselves into the communities that plan and develop applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain regular environmental scanning (e.g., Horizon Report), compile and disseminate findings, and participate in developer/open-source communities to influence roadmaps and build organizational knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governance body: purpose and vision review frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: A governance body is needed that deals not only with current issues related to online systems, but also provides a forum for discussion of emerging trends, organizes meetings and events to share and demonstrate new ideas, and revisits the vision for the online learning system regularly (e.g., every year or two).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a governance forum that balances short-term operational issues with long-term strategic vision, and schedule regular vision reviews to inform planning and budgets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governance membership criteria and diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: A more important criterion for membership for such an expert, however, is an individual’s willingness to consider a wide variety of alternatives, and to not stubbornly defend their own particular preferred approach. In addition, users of the online systems, neophyte teachers, students, and user support staff, provide an important balance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select members who are open-minded, include technical experts plus novice users and support staff, and chair the body at a high management level to ensure authority and balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governance authority in resource allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: The governance body also plays an important role in the allocation of resources to specific initiatives. Such decision-making ability and authority is essential to effective governance; a broad strategic perspective should be channelled through the governance body to prioritize and allocate limited resources to projects with the most potential to achieve the institution’s objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the governance body has clear authority and criteria to fund initiatives strategically rather than allowing local or individual biases to dominate funding decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-level governance with defined acceptance criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Governance, therefore, should have three levels of decision-making: enterprise, departmental, and individual, each level with defined criteria for acceptance, and each level armed with a clear understanding of how the technology will be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define decision thresholds and acceptance criteria at each governance level to enable innovation while ensuring compatibility and supportability across the institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous transparent communication
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirement to continuously communicate at all levels of the organization cannot be overstated. ... The adoption of transparent processes with effective governance provides the basis for developing trusting relationships ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use newsletters, forums, and external channels to broadcast developments; keep language simple and provide opportunities for input and clarification to reduce apprehension about change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pilot projects with clear expectations and arm’s-length evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: An important dimension of change is the use of pilot projects for new developments, plus effective evaluation of their impact before proceeding to wider adoption. Having clear expectations of the pilot communicated to the project owners in advance ... Evaluation of any pilot system should be at arm’s length, and the results should be shared widely throughout the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorize pilots via governance, allocate a resource pool, set well-defined pilot goals and exit criteria, evaluate independently, and publicly share findings to inform scaling decisions and avoid unplanned operational rollouts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change management resourcing and coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: New ideas and approaches must be fostered, not only by words, but also by financial and in-kind resources. Moreover, these resources must be coordinated via an open and widely representative governance body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide funding and non-monetary support aligned with governance priorities; balance organizational control with space for experimentation; recognize and reward contributions to implementation and innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defined change process and project management practices
rubrics_metrics.description: A defined process must also be employed to provide a framework for any proposed changes. ... project management provides transferable practices which can be used for this purpose ... The process must also allow broad input into both the approval process and the precise specifications of the desired change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt project-management frameworks for scope, specification, approvals and stakeholder input to manage complexity from in-house module development to turnkey deployments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usability and people-centered focus for change
rubrics_metrics.description: All change initiatives therefore need to have the usability of the system as their main goal and focus on organizational change; in other words, in the people, not the functionality of a particular piece of technological wizardry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize designs and rollouts that accommodate the capabilities of the weakest users; an adequate, well-accepted technology is better than a superior technology that users cannot or will not use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align infrastructure with curriculum goals and student needs
rubrics_metrics.description: a clear understanding of the goals of the curriculum and the characteristics of the intended students’ needs, coupled with a healthy working environment with committed staff, where implementation can proceed and where constant change is understood to be the norm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base infrastructure decisions on pedagogical goals and the target learner profile before choosing technologies; learn from established examples rather than experimenting haphazardly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimedia selection and bandwidth considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Multimedia incorporates text, graphics, and audio media (often with real video or animations) ... Internet connection speeds limit the quality and quantity of what can be transmitted. ... With the introduction of streaming multimedia ... large multimedia files can now be delivered even over modem connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose multimedia formats and delivery methods (e.g., streaming) appropriate to users' bandwidth and device capabilities; consider compression, format conversion, and player compatibility when planning multimedia materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streaming audio: compression and format compatibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When a sound file is prepared for streaming, it is compressed to reduce the overall size of the file. ... Different programs are available for receiving streaming audio, each with its own proprietary sound or media format. Quality varies from format to format, but all are compatible with modem connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance compression and audio quality for learning purposes; prefer broadly supported formats or provide players that decode multiple formats to reduce user friction. Use streaming for recorded lectures, interviews, and student samples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streaming video: file size, processing demands, and modular content
rubrics_metrics.description: Video files are much larger than audio files, and video combined with audio is larger still. Video samples also demand more processing power on the part of the receiving computer. ... This technique is now driving the creation of modular, chunk-sized content objects ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of file sizes and client processing capabilities; consider chunking video into learning objects, use smaller resolutions where necessary, and implement video where it demonstrably enhances learning rather than as filler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audio chat and VoIP: quality constraints and pedagogical uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the robustness of Internet phone calls, or Voice-over Internet Protocol (VoIP), is currently somewhat inferior to that of dial-up long-distance telephone, consumers are increasingly attracted to Internet telephony. ... conversations can be subject to delays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess bandwidth and latency constraints before adopting VoIP; use for intercultural exchanges, language practice, tutor-student discussions, and combine with electronic blackboards for audio-graphic teleconferencing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Web conferencing for real-time collaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Web conferencing is a form of graphic teleconferencing, used in combination with VoIP as a single tool in general web applications that support real-time collaboration. The “whiteboarding” feature emulates writing or drawing on a blackboard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use web conferencing (whiteboards, application sharing, small video windows) to emulate classroom interactions and for brainstorming; consider license limits, simultaneous logins, and bandwidth when selecting providers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instant messaging as an immediate-contact tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Instant messaging ... strength lies in its ability to facilitate immediate contact with other students and teachers, or with a tutor who is supervising chat sessions. Instant messaging has not yet been used as an efficient content-delivery teaching tool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy IM for quick communications, coordination, and tutor support, but not as a primary method for structured content delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hand-held and wireless technologies: mobile-first planning and accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Hand-held devices are very powerful small computers. ... As affordable access to high bandwidth increases, and the cost of wireless devices ... decreases, the educational possibilities are unlimited. Learning becomes universally accessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan course materials and library access for mobile devices; anticipate cross-device compatibility, lower-bandwidth formats, and opportunities to improve accessibility (e.g., delivering grammar courses or reading rooms to mobile users in low-resource settings).
